introduction: The guide begins with a definition that leaves little room: to be accounted a Bahá’í a person must live by the teachings, be kind to all the inhabitants of the earth and become a cause of general welfare. The badge is conduct. From there these readings ask for words that become deeds, forbearance with the unendurable, silence about others’ faults, honesty in trade and office, courage before rulers, and a character by which a stranger in any city could tell what a believer is. The same demand has been made of every faith by its own scriptures. James asks to be shown faith by works, the Gospel gives love as the mark of a disciple, the Qur’an asks why people say what they do not do, the Dhammapada speaks of a fragrance that travels against the wind. And the demand has its critics and its dangers, which are placed here beside it: Paul’s justification by faith, the Pharisee thankful that he is not as other men, the First Letter of John on those who say they have no sin, Acton on what office does to motives, Dostoevsky on loving humanity and not one’s neighbour, Wollstonecraft on a single virtue named as women’s own. The readings ask to be judged by what they produce, and this company helps to say what that would be.
questions: “Its proof lies in deeds and conduct.” Set this beside James and beside Paul’s “justified by faith without the deeds of the law”. What are deeds evidence of, and for whom?
The readings ask believers to be silent about others’ faults and to endure the unendurable. What do Leviticus on rebuke, and Dostoevsky on loving humanity in general, each add to that counsel?

Believers are to be distinguished from all other peoples, and known as perfect beings. How do the Pharisee’s prayer, “if we say that we have no sin”, and Kant’s crooked material bear on how such sentences should be read?

The readings ask for sincerity toward rulers and praise those whom no ruler could frighten. With Paul to the Romans, the apostles’ “obey God rather than men” and Thoreau in view, how do the two fit together?
Virtue is to be visible, a fragrance, a radiant face, a candle in every clime. What is the difference between this and doing righteousness “to be seen”? Does Gray’s unseen flower lack anything?

Several readings speak of women’s eloquence, courage and renown, and one names chastity as the luminary of their station. Read them with Proverbs 31, Paul to the Corinthians, Seneca Falls and Wollstonecraft. What picture of a believing woman emerges, and what questions remain?

outside.why: “In order to be accounted as a Bahá’í, he must live in accord with the Teachings.” Paine wanted to be accounted a member of nothing: he professed no church’s creed, and his own mind was his church. Does goodness need a name and a community to belong to?

“The badge of the Bahá’ís must be such conduct, deeds, and manners” as conform to the teachings. The Gospel gave its disciples a badge of the same kind: by this shall all know you, if you have love one to another.
A man who has really been in the rose garden carries its fragrance, and “the people needed no words”. The Dhammapada says of that fragrance that it travels even against the wind.
Faith is hidden in the heart, the reading says; “its proof lies in deeds and conduct”. James makes it a challenge: show me your faith without your works, and I will show you mine by them.

The reading looks to deeds for the proof of faith. Paul’s conclusion in Romans, on which the Reformation turned, is that a person is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. Are the two speaking of the same deeds, and of the same judge?
“Regard faith as a tree: its fruits and leaves … are … truthfulness, trustworthiness.” The Qur’an has the same tree for a good word: its root firm, its branches in heaven, its fruit in every season.
“They must never prefer themselves over anyone else.” Paul asks the Philippians for the same habit of mind: in lowliness, to esteem others better than themselves.
The reading praises one “commanding others to goodness but beginning with their own selves”. The Qur’an rebukes the reverse: do you enjoin righteousness on others and forget yourselves?

“No one in this world can claim any relationship to Me except those who … follow My example.” Told that his mother and brothers were outside, Jesus gave the same definition of kinship: whoever does the will of the Father.

The reading asks that an example be followed “in all their deeds and in their conduct”. Emerson held that there comes a time in everyone’s education when he sees that imitation is suicide. What is the difference between following an example and imitating it?

The good conduct of the friends exalts the Word, the reading says, and misconduct could “cause the destruction of the edifice of the Lord”. Paul charges those who boast of the law and break it with the same damage: the name of God is blasphemed because of them.

“My affliction is not My imprisonment, nor that which hath come upon Me from Mine enemies, but rather the deeds of My loved ones.” The psalmist knew the same wound: an enemy he could have borne, but it was his own companion.
“The hosts which today assist the Truth” are goodly character and deeds. Zechariah was told as much about another small community’s resources: not by might, nor by power.

The readings here repeat that the victorious hosts are character and deeds. Machiavelli’s reading of history is that armed prophets conquer and unarmed ones are destroyed. What would each count as victory?
“It is not and was never permissible to oppose anyone.” The Sermon on the Mount goes as far: resist not evil, and turn the other cheek.
The reading forbids opposing anyone. Confucius would not go so far: injury is to be met with justice, and kindness kept for kindness. Is there an opposition that righteousness itself requires?

“The hosts of God this day are goodly deeds … and the commander of these hosts is the fear of God.” The Letter to the Ephesians equips the same kind of army, piece by piece: truth, righteousness, peace, faith.

The person of disinterested deeds “lives above and beyond the criticism of petty and dwarfed assailers”. Paul says the same of himself, and then takes a step the reading does not: he does not acquit himself either.
The reading describes someone whom censure “does not touch”. Proverbs calls the one who hates reproof brutish. How is a person to tell the petty assailant from the critic who is right?
“Those souls who are of the Kingdom eagerly wish to be of service to the poor.” In Matthew’s scene of judgment that service is the whole test, and it turns out to have been done to the judge.
“Forbearance in the face of anger is among the characteristics of the righteous.” The Qur’an lists it among theirs too: those who control their wrath and forgive.
“Bahá’ís must endure people even when they are unendurable.” Peter proposed a generous limit to forgiveness, seven times, and was given a number that means no limit.

The reading asks for patience with unendurable people. A character in Dostoevsky confesses how the matter usually goes: the more he loves humanity in general, the less he loves man in particular. Why is the particular person so much harder than the principle?
“To be silent concerning the faults of others … To look always at the good and not at the bad.” The Gospel’s reason is a matter of scale: the speck in the brother’s eye, the beam in one’s own.

The reading asks for silence about others’ faults and for helping them “through kindness” to correct them. Leviticus, in the verse before “love thy neighbour”, requires that the neighbour be rebuked and not hated in the heart. When does silence serve the other person, and when does it leave him alone with his fault?
One who is asked to listen to talk against another “must not listen”. The Qur’an gives the reason in an image no one forgets: would any of you eat the flesh of his dead brother?
“Be ye always the bearers of good tidings and spread such news quickly.” Proverbs says what good news is to the one who receives it: cold water to a thirsty soul.
“Every living creature is dear to you and the good of each is sought.” Coleridge’s mariner learned it by killing a bird: he prays best who loves best all things both great and small.
“Hast thou love? Then thy power is irresistible.” Paul puts it negatively and at length: without charity, tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even martyrdom are nothing.

“If they accept office, their motive is to render service to the whole of humanity, not to seek their own self-interest.” Acton, a historian of popes and kings, doubted that motive survives office: power tends to corrupt. What would have to be true of a person, or of an office, for the reading’s sentence to hold?

“In times of tribulation, they must respond to cruelty with faithfulness.” Aesop’s fable of the wind and the sun is the plainest statement of why: the harder the wind blew, the tighter the traveller held his cloak.
The reading hopes for “goodly conduct and sincerity toward rulers and kings”. Paul taught the Christians of Rome the same loyalty, on the ground that the powers that be are ordained of God.
The reading asks sincerity toward rulers. The apostles, ordered by their rulers to be silent, answered that they ought to obey God rather than men. Where does sincerity toward a government end?

For the reading, good conduct toward kings may make a land a paradise. Thoreau held that under a government which imprisons unjustly the place for a just man is also a prison. Can a people be both well-wishers of their rulers and witnesses against them?

The Bahá’ís are to be known as people “whose concern is to serve the common good, not to advance their own interests”. Adam Smith thought the common good is mostly served by people pursuing their own. Which of them is describing what people are, and which what they might be?

The reading lists how a community has come to be known among the nations: upright, patient, upholders of peace. An early Christian apologist described his fellow believers to a pagan in the same way, as citizens who share everything and sojourners who endure everything.
A business partnership is to be “renowned … for … excellence in business dealings”. Leviticus puts honest trade among the holy things: just balances, just weights.
“Train yourselves to be always on time no matter where you are. Be punctual.” Shakespeare gives the maxim to a jealous husband hurrying to catch his wife, which has not stopped it being quoted.
“Be ye … daysprings of trustworthiness among the servants.” The Gospel’s test of trustworthiness is the small thing: faithful in the least, faithful in much.
“We counsel thee and My loved ones to trustworthiness and truthfulness.” The Qur’an commands the plainest form of it: restore deposits to their owners, and judge justly.

“One must be pure and free from all carnal desires. All feelings must be heavenly.” Pascal warns that whoever tries to act the angel acts the brute. How is the purity the reading asks for kept from becoming the pretence Pascal describes?

A Bahá’í must “shine out like a lighted taper—not be darkness upon darkness and yet bear the name”. Juliet thinks a name nothing: the rose would smell as sweet without it. The reading agrees about the rose; what does it still ask of the name?
“Train the children … in divine characteristics.” The proverb promises that such training holds: when he is old he will not depart from it.

“The friends of God [must] be distinguished from all other peoples and tribes in divine virtues.” At Sinai Israel is called to the same distinction: a peculiar treasure, a kingdom of priests, a holy nation.

The reading asks believers to be distinguished from all other peoples. The Pharisee of the parable is distinguished, and knows it: he thanks God that he is not as other men are. How is distinction sought without that prayer?
“He has the power to choose immortal life or to reject it.” Moses sets the same choice before a whole people, life and death, and urges them to choose life.

Man alone, says the reading, can choose immortal life, “while the animals have no qualities that are immortal”. The Preacher is not sure of the difference: one breath, one end, and who knows that the spirit of man goes upward? What does the reading’s account of choice rest on?
“So that the world may know that a Bahá’í is a perfect being.” The Sermon on the Mount sets the same mark, and names the measure: as your Father in heaven is perfect.

“If a soul is not severed, if he is not pure and holy … no one can say he is a Bahá’í.” The First Letter of John warns from the other side: if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. Who, by the reading’s test, could say it of himself?

Before one step forward or back, the reading says, a believer “must first think” whether it serves. Confucius heard of a man who thought three times before acting and said that twice would do. When does deliberation become a way of not acting?
“The disciples of Christ … sold everything they had and went out to preach.” Acts describes the community they formed: one heart, all things common, and no one among them in want.
“Where are they … who were not frightened by the might of kings?” Three of them answer Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel: God can deliver us; but if not, we still will not serve your gods.

“Neither the circumstances of tyrants nor the might of pharaohs deterred” them. Mencius defines the great man by the same three immunities: wealth cannot dissipate him, poverty cannot move him, force cannot bend him.
“The opposition of the world did not hinder them, nor did the might of rulers weaken them.” The psalmist gives the sentence such people say to themselves.

The reading honours those who “were not deterred by the blame of the blameworthy”. Peter promised the same of himself on the night he failed. What do the steadfast know about themselves that Peter did not yet know?

The readings praise those who feared no ruler. Falstaff, having played dead on the battlefield, speaks for everyone else: the better part of valour is discretion, and by it he has saved his life. Is there a discretion that is not his?

“Thou, too, must make a mighty effort and show forth supreme courage.” Joshua, taking over from Moses, is given the same order and its ground: be strong, for the Lord is with thee wherever thou goest.

The reading asks for supreme courage. In Gethsemane the disciples, who meant to be brave, are told to watch and pray, because the spirit is willing and the flesh is weak. What does courage owe to knowing that?
“The very members of your body must bear witness to the loftiness of your purpose.” In the Qur’an the hands and feet do bear witness, on the day when the mouth is sealed.
“Be ye symbols of guidance and lights of godliness.” The Sermon on the Mount says to its hearers that they are the light of the world, and that a city on a hill cannot be hid.
“Our stay here is like unto worship, for … we are occupied with His mention.” The Gospel promises a presence wherever two or three are gathered in that way.
Some souls are like glass chimneys, “pure and transparent but an outside light must come in and illumine them”. Paul’s vessel is plainer still, earthenware, and the treasure in it is not its own.

In the reading the light comes to the glass from outside. The Buddha’s last counsel to his disciples was to be lamps to themselves and to look for no external refuge. Where does each locate the source of a person’s light?

The cup of nearness is reserved for those “who have had and have no will or desire of their own”. A soul in Dante’s paradise says the same of all the blessed: their wishes are made one with the will divine, and in that will is their peace.
The reading praises those with no will of their own. Polonius puts being true to one’s own self above all. Which self does each have in view, and can a person have both?

A believer must so walk “that all will testify to his sanctity and detachment”. Gray’s flower is as sweet and no one testifies to it at all. Is a virtue the less for being unseen, and why do the readings want it seen?
“That all may inhale from them the fragrance of the love of God.” Paul uses the same sense for the same thing: we are a sweet savour of Christ in every place.

The firm ones must show “such qualities and virtues as to astonish minds and amaze souls”, so that the world knows what they are. The Gospel warns against doing righteousness “to be seen”. What keeps the wish to be known as well-wishers from spoiling the well-wishing?
“Their faces are radiant.” Moses came down from Sinai with a shining face and did not know it; the others saw.
“Their souls are intimate and harmonious with each other.” The psalm of ascents says simply how good and pleasant that is.
These are servants “whom the affairs of men sadden not” and whom clamour does not frighten. The Qur’an says of the friends of God that no fear comes upon them, nor do they grieve.

The servants in the reading “speak not except by His leave” and “move not except by His command”. Emerson saw every society as a conspiracy against the independence of its members and asked for self-reliance. Is obedience to God, as the reading means it, a form of the conformity he attacked or its opposite?
What befits believers is to appear “with goodly and pleasing character. This is the cause of the exaltation of God’s Cause.” A saying of Muḥammad makes good character the purpose of his mission.
“Blessed are they who have cast away what they possessed.” A rich young man was offered that blessing in so many words and went away sorrowful.

The reading blesses those who regard “all else save God as non-existent and null”. The Preacher finds it good and comely to eat, drink and enjoy the fruit of one’s labour, as a portion given by God. Can what God gives be null?
“Perform such deeds as will cause the exaltation of the Cause.” James asks for doers of the word, and compares the mere hearer to a man who forgets his own face.

The people of a city should be able to say, “This man is unquestionably a Bahá’í.” The council in Jerusalem recognized two fishermen the same way: by their boldness they knew that they had been with Jesus.
A person is to be known for sincerity, honesty and loving-kindness. King’s dream for his children was a country that would judge them so, by the content of their character.
The beloved “burn like bright candles in every clime”. Portia notices how far one candle carries at night, and thinks of a good deed.

“They reform morals … engaging in purification of hearts and refinement of souls.” Aristotle says how a character is in fact formed: by doing the acts, as builders learn by building. Does the refinement of souls begin within and work outward, or the other way?
“This prisoner is grateful and pleased … and is joyful day and night remembering them.” Paul, also a prisoner, begins a letter to his friends at Philippi in the same words.
A man who had known youth in pleasure and age in destitution endured “with utmost thankfulness”. Paul says he had to learn that: how to be abased and how to abound.
The reading remembers a believer who lost everything and remained thankful. Job’s words on the day of his losses are the pattern.

“In deeds they are like heavenly angels.” Kant doubted that such a thing can be said of anyone: from the crooked material of which man is made, nothing quite straight is built. How should praise of this kind be heard?
A servant of God is one who “through deeds, behavior and words gives news of the Kingdom”. The First Letter of John asks for love in that order: not in word, but in deed and in truth.

“They regard strangers as friends and consider foreigners as familiar ones.” The Letter to the Hebrews gives hospitality to strangers a surprising motive: some have entertained angels without knowing it.
“That one person has formed such a family is the pure grace of the living God.” Joshua speaks for his household in the same spirit: as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.

The reading rejoices in a family united in faith. The Gospel warns that faith can as easily divide one, son against father and daughter against mother. What makes the difference between the two outcomes?
Women believers should be known for “articulate speech, an eloquent tongue … and high resolve”. The good wife of Proverbs is clothed in strength and honour and opens her mouth with wisdom.

The reading wants women to “stand out and achieve renown”, with eloquent tongues. Paul’s rule for the church at Corinth was that they keep silence. How did communities that read both come to choose between them?

“If the son walks in the steps of the father, then the relationship of sonship is real.” Ezekiel insists that each stands alone before God: the son does not carry the father’s guilt, nor the father the son’s. What does a child inherit, and what must each generation do for itself?

The reading values “noble blood … joined with a goodly character”. Burns will not allow blood any share: rank is the stamp on the coin, and the man is the gold. Does lineage add anything to character?
“She communed with Thee evening and morning.” Luke remembers such a woman by name: Anna, a widow of great age, who served God with fastings and prayers night and day.

The living are to act so that a departed spirit “will open his tongue in praise” and be gladdened. The Letter to the Hebrews also pictures the faithful dead as watching: a cloud of witnesses around those still running the race.

“Thank the Lord that thou art born of a father who is pure and a mother who is chaste and … raised in the cradle of belief.” Paul reminds Timothy of the same inheritance: a faith that lived first in his grandmother and his mother.

The heaven of women’s station, says the reading, “hath been and shall ever be illumined by one luminary, and that is chastity”. The women at Seneca Falls began from the equality of women and men in every right. What does it do to women to have one virtue named as theirs?

The reading names chastity as the single luminary of women’s station. Wollstonecraft objected to exactly this in her own society: when a woman’s reputation is confined to one virtue, she may neglect every other duty and still be called honourable. Does the reading escape her objection?

He “called others to Your remembrance … until his spirit … soared to the center of grace”. Paul’s summary of his own life is the model for such epitaphs: a good fight, a finished course, the faith kept.
“We should do so with a candle in our hand.” The wise virgins of the parable are the ones whose lamps have oil when the hour comes.

The reading hopes to leave this world carrying a candle, with brightness and spirit. For Macbeth life itself is the candle, and it goes out: a walking shadow, a tale signifying nothing. What does the reading hold that he has lost?
